newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy finally resolves long metalworkers' pay row.
newsitem.headline: Italy finally resolves long metalworkers' pay row.

text.p: Italian metalworkers unions and employers signed a government-brokered deal on Tuesday, ending a bitter months-long pay dispute in the key industrial sector.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who intervened directly to resolve the damaging dispute, hailed the agreement "with extreme satisfaction" as a success in his plan to renew Italy.
"By ending the metalworkers' dispute, the country has taken another decisive step towards a future of stability," Prodi said in a statement after the deal was signed at the Labour Ministry.
"It was a difficult contract that couldn't satisfy everyone completely," Labour Minister Tiziano Treu said.
"But I am satisfied because just 24 hours ago, there were still doubts."

Pay awards for the country's 1.7 million engineering and metalworkers have been in limbo since two-year contracts ran out in June. The sector, which includes Italy's biggest company Fiat, accounts for 40 percent of Italy's industrial output.

The FIM, FIOM and UILM unions have been at loggerheads with employers' group Federmeccanica ever since June and have staged a number of strikes to press for their claim for higher wages to compensate for inflation.

Federmeccanica staunchly resisted union demands and a first pay proposal from the government before reluctantly agreeing to the deal which forces them to pay out a lump-sum and a series of gradual pay rises over the course of a new 30-month contract.
"This is a deal which leaves everyone both satisfied and dissatisfied," Federmeccanica director-general Michele Figurati said. "Let's hope we can do better next time."

The dispute, one of Italy's most bitter recent industrial battles, has been closely watched by financial markets as it is expected to set the tone for pay accords in other sectors and prove key to Italy's hopes of keeping a tight lid on inflation.

Analysts say markets have already accepted that the deal will not fuel inflation and Italian shares ended firm on expectations the deal was imminent. Consumer prices data published earlier on Tuesday showed inflation running at 2.6 percent year-on-year in January, unchanged from December.

The government-brokered deal is based on a one-off payment of 512,000 lire ($316), paid in two instalments to cover the first six months, followed by graduated monthly wage increases totalling 200,000 lire ($124) during the rest of the contract.

Italy's employers umbrella group Confindustria said in a statement that it was satisfied such a long and difficult chapter had now been closed without giving into the "exorbitant demands" of union leaders.

But it said it was worried that the pay rise foreseen under the deal, which it said was equivalent to seven percent over the 30-month life of the contract, was above inflation especially when internal company agreements were taken into account.
"Confindustria underlines that this cycle of bargaining is unrepeatable," the statement said, adding that the sector should now concentrate on regaining its competitiveness.
